press_records.headline: Life Savers Holes Pulled From Stores Due to Packaging Fears
key_facts: Introduced in late 1990; roughly 40 million packages sold by early 1991.
Voluntarily recalled after four instances where children or teenagers bit off the dime-sized plastic flip-top cap and swallowed or gagged on it.
Choking hazard stemmed from the plastic flip-top cap on the tube rather than the candy itself.

dossiers.title: Nestle Magic Ball

press_records.headline: NESTLE TO STOP SELLING 'MAGIC' CANDY THAT DREW SAFETY OBJECTIONS
key_facts: Launched in summer 1997 as a hollow milk-chocolate sphere containing a plastic Disney toy figurine inside.
Voluntarily pulled in October 1997 following FDA objections and pressure from 14 state attorneys general and Mars Inc.

press_records.headline: Nestle Magic: Now You See It; Now You Don't--Ever Again
key_facts: FDA held that the product violated Section 402(d)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938.
Relaunched in April 2000 as the Wonder Ball with edible candy pieces inside instead of plastic toys.

press_records.headline: Nestle Chocolate Balls Lose Disney Magic
key_facts: Covered the withdrawal of the Disney-themed chocolate surprise balls.

dossiers.title: Taco Bell Home Originals Taco Shells (StarLink Corn)
dossiers.company: Kraft Foods (Taco Bell brand) / Aventis CropScience

press_records.headline: Biotech Critics Cite Unapproved Corn in Taco Shells
key_facts: Independent lab tests commissioned by environmental groups found genetically modified StarLink corn (Cry9C protein) in Taco Bell Home Originals taco shells.
StarLink corn was approved by the EPA strictly for animal feed and industrial use, not for human food, due to potential allergenicity concerns.
Kraft Foods issued a nationwide recall of Taco Bell Home Originals 12 Taco Shells, 18 Taco Shells, and Taco Dinner — the first-ever recall of a GMO food.

key_quotes: first-ever recall of a genetically engineered (GMO) food

dossiers.title: Odwalla Unpasteurized Apple Juice (E. coli O157:H7)

press_records.headline: Fruit Juices Linked to E. Coli Outbreak
key_facts: On October 31, 1996, Odwalla initiated a voluntary nationwide recall of all juice products containing unpasteurized apple juice.
The E. coli O157:H7 outbreak sickened at least 70 people across Washington, California, Colorado, and British Columbia; 25 were hospitalized, 14 developed HUS, and a 16-month-old toddler died.
In 1998, Odwalla pleaded guilty to 16 federal criminal charges and paid a $1.5 million fine; the company switched to flash pasteurization.

regulatory_references.quote: WARNING: This product has not been pasteurized and therefore may contain harmful bacteria that can cause serious illness in children, the elderly, and persons with weakened immune systems.

key_quotes: WARNING: This product has not been pasteurized and therefore may contain harmful bacteria that can cause serious illness in children, the elderly, and persons with weakened immune systems.
